move: Diagnoses the Hegelian identification of contradictories as a self-consuming movement toward ever more abstract unity, without addressing whether a self endures.

Argues that an image considered in itself is identical whether referred to past, present, or future, so the resulting emotion is the same — a claim about the timelessness of images rather than about an enduring self.
Explains the seeming constancy of forms as mere appearance, since every individual and every part of every individual is perpetually changing while the whole only looks the same.
Holds that the mind endeavours to persist in its own being for an indefinite rather than a limited time, and is conscious of that endeavour through the ideas of its body's modifications.

Distinguishes practical union with God from substantial identity, insisting the subject remains a distinct numerical fact of existence — a point about self versus divinity, not about endurance through time.
Identifies the endeavour by which each thing persists in its own being with its actual essence, and asserts that this endeavour involves no finite but an indefinite time.
Reports the doctrine of a being fixed in one simple perfect state, with no succession, change, or diversity, without endorsing or applying it to the human self.

Explains why remembered evils give pleasure, by the image reviving the old determination to pain while associated images excluding the thing's existence check it — an account of memory's affect, not of personal identity.

Treats cause, necessity, number, and law as symbols we ourselves devised and then mythologically project onto things in themselves, and recasts talk of unfree will as a matter of strong and weak wills.
Unpacks 'I think' into a series of unproved assertions — that it is I who think, that something must think, that there is an 'ego' — denying any immediate certainty of a thinking subject.

Argues that if time belongs to things in themselves, self-consciousness would make one a thinking automaton whose sense of spontaneity is delusion, pressing the point about freedom rather than about an enduring self.
Recounts an intoxication in which ego and object, meum and tuum, seemed one and unbroken continuity appeared to be the essence of being, offering the experience as a datum rather than an argument.
